media.caption: A roofed building on a platform, possibly once an incense-burner lid. Current catalogue: 200 BCE–200 CE. Three numbered modern notes point to visible architecture on the unchanged photograph; they do not reconstruct missing rooms or prove the proposed use.
notice: What makes the proposed function more than a visual observation?
media.creator: Maker not recorded
media.relevance: Compare architectural form and tentative use with the Han tower without asserting contact.
media.datingNote: Current catalogue: 200 BCE–200 CE. Pillsbury’s 2015 essay captions the same accession 200 BCE–300 CE. Current catalogue followed; discrepancy preserved.
additionalImageAlts: Frontal view of the peaked roof and the short stairway ascending the platform between two raised corner features.

annotations.rights: Modern annotations: CC BY 4.0. The underlying photograph has separate credit and rights.

items.label: A peaked roof
items.text: Two sloping surfaces meet at the roof’s high point. The catalogue calls this a temple model; this photograph does not identify a surviving full-size building or the roof’s original building material.

items.label: An opening beneath the roof
items.text: An open front lets us see space beneath the roof. No figure or complete ceremony is supplied by this view. The proposed incense-burner-lid use comes from the catalogue, rather than being proved by the opening alone.

citations.locator: Description; existing main photograph, open front

items.label: A raised platform
items.text: The roofed structure stands above a broad ceramic platform, with a small stair at its front. This makes levels and access visible in miniature; it does not supply an architectural scale, a known tomb or the missing body of a burner.

citations.locator: Description; existing main photograph, platform and stair
